questions.question: What is a method set in Go?
questions.title: Method Sets
questions.direct_answer: The set of methods a TYPE has, determining interface satisfaction. For type T: methods with receiver T. For *T: methods with receiver T AND *T. The rule that decides whether your type satisfies an interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Method Sets beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: The set of methods a TYPE has, determining interface satisfaction. For type T: methods with receiver T.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A method set is exactly what satisfies an interface — the compiler checks 'does this value's type have every interface method?' and the method set is the answer for each type:

```go
func (u User) Greet() string   // in User's method set AND *User's
func (u *User) Inc()          // in *User's method set ONLY
```

The rule with its consequence: *User's method set is a superset (both Greet and Inc); User's is Greet only. So *User satisfies any interface needing Greet or Inc; User satisfies only Greet-interfaces. The pointer can do everything the value can plus more.

Executed proof of the asymmetry: a pointer p := &u can call p.Greet() (value method on pointer — works, auto-dereference) AND p.Inc(); the bare value u can call u.Greet() but User{Name:"x"}.Inc() is a compile error — 'cannot call pointer method Inc on U' — because the method set of the VALUE doesn't include pointer-receiver methods.

Why the asymmetry exists: a pointer receiver means 'this method may modify the receiver' — which requires the method to have the receiver's address. A pointer has one; a bare value might not (temporaries, map elements — non-addressable storage). Rather than a silent auto-address in SOME contexts and not others, the rule is uniform: pointer-receiver methods live in the pointer's method set, period. The compiler's auto-addressing for addressable values (u.Inc() on a variable works — it's (&u).Inc()) is a CALL-SITE convenience, not a method-set change — and that distinction is exactly what trips the map-element case.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    V[User value] --> MS1[method set: value receivers only]
    P[*User pointer] --> MS2[method set: value + pointer receivers]
    MS1 --> I1[satisfies Greet-interface]
    MS2 --> I1
    MS2 --> I2[satisfies Inc-interface — value CANNOT]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The method-set rule is arbitrary-looking until you trace the addressability reasoning, and the follow-up: WHY does u.Inc() compile when u is a variable, if Inc isn't in User's method set? Because the CALL rule and the METHOD SET rule are different rules:

Call rule: for an addressable value u, u.Inc() is shorthand for (&u).Inc() — the compiler takes the address, the method set of *User applies. For a NON-addressable value (map lookup result, function return, struct field of a non-addressable), the shorthand can't exist — no address exists — so the call is a compile error.

Method-set rule (interface satisfaction): does NOT apply call-site shorthands. An interface holding a User value has the User's method set — Greet, no Inc — regardless of where the value came from. This is why storing User values in an []Greeter works while []Incrementer rejects them: the method set is a property of the TYPE, frozen at the value's creation, not enhanced by the context of use.

The map-element proof that the two rules diverge: m[k].Inc() — m[k] is addressable-for-read but not writable-addressable (map internals move elements) — the call rule cannot apply its shorthand — compile error with the message 'cannot call pointer method on U' — the method set was never the issue; the address was.

The design coherence: Go wanted pointer receivers to be a real semantic statement (mutation capability) without making interfaces unpredictable. Method sets make interface satisfaction decidable from types alone; call shorthand keeps the ergonomics; addressability defines exactly where the shorthand may fire. Three rules, one coherent system — and interviewers probe exactly the seams (map elements, temporaries) where the rules must be applied separately.

questions.question: What is the difference between value receivers and pointer receivers?
questions.title: When would you use Method Sets in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Value receiver (u User): gets a COPY — mutations don't escape. Pointer receiver (u *User): gets the address — mutations persist. Rule of thumb: pointer when you mutate, when the struct is large, or for consistency with other methods; value for small immutable data.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Value receiver (u User): gets a COPY — mutations don't escape. Pointer receiver (u *User): gets the address — mutations persist.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two receiver declarations and what each one means:

```go
func (u User) Greet() string { return "hi " + u.Name }  // value: works on a copy
func (u *User) Inc()       { u.Age++ }                  // pointer: works on the original
```

Executed asymmetry: after p := &u; p.Inc(), the original u.Age changed (verified: 30 → 31). A Greet on u or p — same result, no visible difference, because Greet doesn't mutate.

When to choose which — the decision list, in order:

1. Mutate the receiver? Pointer. The only way the change survives the call.
2. Struct large? Pointer. A value receiver copies the whole struct on every call — an 8-field struct with a map and slices copies three words (headers), but a 64-field data struct copying per call is real cost. The runtime number to know: value receivers pass by copy — cost proportional to struct size; pointers pass one word.
3. Consistency: a type with ONE pointer method should make them all pointer — mixing receiver kinds makes the method-set behavior confusing (some methods in the interface-satisfying set, some not).
4. Value receivers for: small structs, immutable-by-design types, methods on maps/slices/funcs — where the type itself is a reference and copying is trivial.

The trap the receiver kind sets: value receivers satisfy interfaces from BOTH User and *User; pointer receivers only from *User — the method-set rule from the previous question. So a type whose mutation methods are pointer-receiver can't be stored by value in interfaces needing those methods — an interface design consequence hiding in a receiver choice.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The copy mechanics, one layer down: a value receiver method call compiles to the method receiving a fresh copy of the struct — stack storage for the parameter, contents copied at call time. The copy is shallow — reference-typed fields (slices, maps, pointers) copy their HEADERS, pointing at the same underlying data. So a value receiver CAN mutate a slice's elements (u.Tags[0] = "x" writes through the shared array) but can't replace the field itself (u.Tags = nil changes only the copy's header). That half-mutation is the most common value-receiver bug: the author thinks 'value = safe from mutation' and writes through an embedded reference — mutation escapes anyway.

The pointer receiver's dereference cost: negligible (one memory indirection) — and often NET CHEAPER than a large value copy. The performance folklore 'pointers are for big structs' has the direction right: the crossover is where the copy cost exceeds one indirection — for small structs (a few words), value receivers can actually be FASTER (no indirection, better locality, escape analysis can keep everything in registers).

The escape-analysis interaction nobody mentions: a pointer receiver means the receiver's address escapes into the method call — which can force heap allocation of the receiver variable if the method (or anything it calls) stores the pointer. A value receiver on a small struct stays stack-local more easily. 'All pointer receivers' as a style rule has a cost: it can quietly push allocations up in tight loops — one reason the standard library mixes deliberately (time.Time's methods are value receivers — small, immutable, allocation-conscious).

The receiver choice is also API documentation: a value receiver tells the caller 'calling this changes nothing on the original' — a contract the compiler enforces. Pointer receivers say 'this may modify' — readers check. That signal is why consistency matters beyond tidiness: a type with mixed receivers forces readers to check each method's kind, per call, to know what might change.

questions.question: Why can't you call pointer methods on some values?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Method Sets
questions.direct_answer: Non-addressable values: map elements, function returns, temporary literals. The call needs the receiver's address to pass; non-addressable storage has none. Variables and slice elements ARE addressable — the shorthand works there.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Non-addressable values: map elements, function returns, temporary literals. The call needs the receiver's address to pass; non-addressable storage has none.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The error, verbatim (executed): 'cannot call pointer method Inc on U' — triggered when the receiver expression can't be address-taken:

```go
m := map[string]User{"x": {Age: 1}}
m["x"].Inc()        // compile error — m["x"] is non-addressable

User{Name: "t", Age: 1}.Inc()  // compile error — a temporary

u := User{Age: 1}
u.Inc()             // works — u is a variable (addressable)
s := []User{{Age: 1}}
s[0].Inc()         // works — slice elements are addressable
```

The rule the compiler implements: x.Inc() (pointer method) on a value x compiles only when x is addressable — because the call needs (&x).Inc(), and &x requires a real storage location. Variables, slice elements, struct fields reachable through addressable chains — all have addresses. Map values, function returns, expression temporaries — the storage either isn't stable (map internals move elements during growth) or never existed as a named location.

Why map elements specifically: the map's hash table can relocate entries (growth, evacuation) — an address into it would dangle. That's the same reason map values can't be taken as & at all. The workarounds each express the real fix — take the value out, modify, put back:

```go
u := m["x"]    // copy out
u.Inc()       // mutate the copy
m["x"] = u   // store back
```

or store pointers in the map (map[string]*User) — the map's VALUES are pointer headers (stable to copy), the pointees live at fixed heap addresses, and m["x"].Inc() works because the address being taken is the POINTER variable's target, not a map slot.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q[the question] --> R[the core rule]
    R --> EX[the small example]
    EX --> B[the boundary — where the rule ends]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Addressability is a property of EXPRESSIONS, not types — the spec's concept that ties this together. An expression is addressable if it denotes a stable storage location: variables (always), pointer dereferences (*p — the pointee is addressable through p), slice indexing (s[i] — the array slot), field selectors through addressable chains (u.Field, s[0].Field). Not addressable: map indexing (the slot can move), function/method return values (temporary), composite literals in expressions (temporary), constants (no storage).

The unify rule: &x is legal exactly when x is addressable — and x.PtrMethod() needs (&x) — so the set of legal pointer-method calls IS the addressable set. That's why the errors group the way they do, and why the fix is always 'get the value into a variable' (a variable being the canonical addressable thing).

The pointer-in-the-map pattern's mechanics: map[string]*User stores one-word pointer values. m["x"] returns a copy of the POINTER (cheap, stable) — the pointer value is addressable as a map value? No — but it doesn't need to be: the method call needs the RECEIVER's address, and the receiver *User is a pointer already — its address (the pointee's address) exists in the heap regardless of where the map's copy of the pointer lives. The non-addressability of map values applies to the POINTER variable — but pointer methods on a pointer receiver don't need the variable's address, they need the pointee — heap-stable. That's the deep reason map[string]*User + pointer methods just works.

The escape-analysis coda: addressable locals + pointer methods = the receiver's address escapes into the call — the compiler must keep the variable somewhere with a stable address for the call's duration. Usually stack; heap if the method stores the pointer. Non-addressable receivers would break this model (a temporary's 'address' would have to be the call frame — which is why temporaries simply can't take pointer methods; there's no stable there to point at).

questions.question: How do methods attach to types in Go, and can you add methods to types you don't own?
questions.title: compare Method Sets with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: Methods are declared ONCE, attached to a receiver type defined in the same package. You cannot add methods to types from other packages — that's why wrapper types exist.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: Methods are declared ONCE, attached to a receiver type defined in the same package. You cannot add methods.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The receiver clause binds a function to a type:

```go
func (u User) Greet() string { ... }
//  ^ receiver: this method now belongs to User
```

The one rule that governs where methods can be declared: the receiver's base type must be defined in the SAME PACKAGE as the method. You can extend your own types; you cannot open someone else's — no adding HeadCount() to []string or io.Reader.

The reason is coherence: method sets are a compile-time contract per package. If any package could add methods to any type, then io.Reader could have a different method set in every program — interface satisfaction would depend on import graphs, compile determinism would die, and two packages adding the same method name would conflict with no resolution rule. Go closes the whole problem at the root.

The idiom that replaces 'just add a method': the wrapper type — define a new type in YOUR package with the underlying type, and attach methods there:

```go
type UserIDs []string           // new type, your package
func (u UserIDs) Dedupe() UserIDs { ... }   // your methods on it
```

type UserIDs []string is a NEW type (not an alias) — it has []string's underlying structure and zero of its methods (a defined type starts with an EMPTY method set). That's deliberate: the wrapper doesn't inherit []string's methods either — it's a fresh surface, yours to build.

The alias (type U = User — Go 1.9+) is the other direction: SAME type, both names usable interchangeably — aliases for compatibility and refactoring, not for method attachment (there's nothing to attach — it's one type).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q[the question] --> R[the core rule]
    R --> EX[the small example]
    EX --> B[the boundary — where the rule ends]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The same-package rule's exact boundary: 'the receiver type must be defined in the same package as the method declaration' — the SPEC says its underlying type must not be a pointer or interface type and must be declared in the same package. The interesting edges:

- You CAN define methods on named types whose underlying type comes from elsewhere: type MyList = ... no — type MyList []int (defined in your package, underlying []int is builtin): methods attach to MyList freely. The rule is about WHERE THE TYPE IS DEFINED, not where its structure came from.
- Embedding partially reopens extension: embed []*User in your type and your type has promoted methods... only the ones on []*User (which its package already defined). You route to existing methods; you add none to the inner.
- Generic type parameters (1.18+): methods on generic types are declared with the receiver carrying the parameterization: func (l List[T]) Push(v T) — the method is on List[T], your defined type, same-package rule unchanged.

The empty-method-set property of defined types deserves its own note, because it surprises: type MyReader io.Reader — defined type from an interface — has NO methods (not even Read). Its method set is empty until you build it — you're expected to embed io.Reader INSIDE it (the delegation pattern) if you want forwarding. The one exception in the language: embedded interfaces' methods promote into the outer STRUCT — but that's struct embedding, a different mechanism from type definition.

Why the design chose this over extension methods (C#) or categories (Objective-C / Rust traits): Go's method set must be closed — visible from the package alone — for separate compilation (compile a package knowing its types' full surfaces without reading the universe), for interface determinism (satisfaction checkable locally), and for security (no smuggling methods onto types across trust boundaries). The cost — wrapper boilerplate — buys compile determinism, and the ecosystem's shape (small interfaces + adapters + wrappers) grew from that trade.

questions.question: Can a method modify its receiver? What decides?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Method Sets
questions.direct_answer: Pointer receiver (u *User): modifications persist — the method holds the receiver's address. Value receiver (u User): modifications die with the copy — the original is untouched. The receiver kind IS the modification contract.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Pointer receiver (u *User): modifications persist — the method holds the receiver's address. Value receiver (u User): modifications die with the copy — the original is untouched.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The receiver kind is the entire answer, and the executed proof is three lines:

```go
func (u User)  Rename(s string) { u.Name = s }  // value: copy's name changes
func (u *User) RenamePtr(s string) { u.Name = s } // pointer: original changes

u := User{Name: "Al"}
u.Rename("Bo")
fmt.Println(u.Name)   // "Al" — the value receiver's change is gone
p := &u
p.RenamePtr("Cy")
fmt.Println(u.Name)   // "Cy" — the pointer receiver's change persists
```

The mechanics: the value receiver's method body operates on a copy made at call time — every field write lands in the copy's storage, which evaporates at return. The pointer receiver's body dereferences to the caller's actual variable — writes land in the original.

The half-mutation trap (worth its own mention in any answer): the value receiver's copy is SHALLOW — a slice field's elements are shared with the original. u.Tags[0] = "x" through a VALUE receiver mutates the original's slice contents (same backing array) — while u.Tags = append(...) rebinds only the copy's header. So 'value receivers can't modify' needs its precise form: they can't modify the RECEIVER (the struct's own fields), but writes through the receiver's reference-typed fields DO escape. That escape is the #1 value-receiver bug in real code.

The interface consequence connects to method sets: a type whose mutating methods are pointer receivers can only satisfy interfaces AS THE POINTER — []Incrementer can't hold User values (Inc isn't in User's method set). The modification decision cascades: receiver kind → method set → interface satisfaction → what the type can be stored in.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The compiler's view of the two receivers, because it explains every behavior:

Value: the call passes the struct's CONTENTS as the argument — same as any by-value parameter. The method's u is a fresh stack slot (or register-passed struct), constructed by copying the caller's value. Mutation is impossible BY CONSTRUCTION — the method has no reference to the original.

Pointer: the call passes ONE WORD — the address. The method's u is that address; every field access is u.Name compiling to (*u).Name — an indirection to the caller's storage. Mutation is possible BY CONSTRUCTION — the original is reachable.

The shallow-copy subtlety mechanically: the value receiver's copy duplicates each FIELD — a slice field's header (pointer, len, cap) is copied, so both the original and the copy hold pointers to the SAME backing array. Indexed writes go through the shared array (visible both ways); the copy's header rebinding (append, assignment) is private. This is why 'does the value receiver protect me?' has the answer 'structurally yes, referentially no' — the protection is exactly one layer deep.

Escape analysis interacts once more: a pointer receiver forces the method to hold the receiver's address — if the caller's value was a temporary that the compiler materialized for the call, it now needs a stable address (a real allocation, potentially heap). The ubiquitous 'methods on large structs should use pointer receivers' performance rule is really this: copy cost (value) versus indirection + possible allocation forcing (pointer). For immutable small structs — time.Time at 24 bytes — value receivers win on every axis; the standard library's receiver choices are a curated exhibit of the trade.
